front: What is the same across every branch of a parallel R-C circuit?
Phase of the resistive branch current?
back: In phase with the voltage.

front: Phase of the capacitive branch current?
How many degrees apart are Iᵣ and Ic in parallel?
Does total current lead or lag in parallel R-C?
back: Leads, by an angle between 0° and 90°.

front: What sets the phase angle in parallel R-C?
back: How current splits between branches: tan θ = Ic/Iᵣ = R/Xc.

front: In parallel R-C, does a bigger capacitor make the circuit more or less capacitive?
back: MORE capacitive — lower Xc draws more Ic (opposite of series R-C).
extra_notes: Bigger R also makes it more capacitive

front: In a parallel phasor diagram, what is the reference and which way does Ic point?
back: Voltage is the reference (0°). Ic points UP (leading). Iᵣ lies along E.

front: 30 Ω ∥ Xc 20 Ω on 240 V: branch currents?
Branch current formulas?
Capacitance for Xc = 20 Ω at 60 Hz?
Total current formula in parallel R-C?
Iᵣ = 8 A, Ic = 12 A. Iₜ?
Feeder clamp reads 14.4 A while branches read 8 A and 12 A. Fault?
back: No — the branch currents are 90° apart and add as vectors.

front: Several capacitor branches plus a resistor: how do you get Iₜ?
back: Add the capacitor currents straight (same phase), then Iₜ = √(Iᵣ² + Ic total²).

front: Simplest way to find Z when E and Iₜ are known?

Reciprocal formula for parallel R-C impedance?

Which formula gives Z for 30 Ω ∥ Xc 20 Ω?
back: Only R·Xc/√(R² + Xc²) = 16.64 Ω. √(R² + Xc²) = 36.06 is the series answer; R·Xc/(R + Xc) = 12 ignores the 90°.

front: Can you draw an impedance triangle with R and Xc as legs for a parallel circuit?
back: No — draw the current triangle instead.

PF formulas for parallel R-C?
Why is parallel PF Z/R, not R/Z?
back: Parallel Z < R, so R/Z would exceed 1 — impossible for PF.

front: Why can't voltage ratios give PF in a parallel circuit?
back: Voltage is the same on every branch, so Eᵣ/Eₜ is always 1.

front: Main example θ?
Other trig ratios for θ in parallel R-C?
back: tan θ = Ic/Iᵣ = VARs/P; sin θ = Ic/Iₜ = VARs/VA

front: Given PF and VA, how do you get P and VARs?
back: P = VA × PF; VARs = √(VA² − P²) (or VA × sin θ).

front: How are power-factor correction capacitors connected?
back: In PARALLEL with the load (across the line) — never in series.

front: How does a parallel capacitor reduce feeder current on a motor circuit?
back: Its leading current cancels part of the motor's lagging current; the feeder carries the smaller vector sum.

front: A capacitor uses no watts. Does it draw real line current?
back: Yes — e.g., 132.6 µF on 240 V draws 12 A. Feeders/disconnects are sized at 135% of capacitor rated current (NEC 460.8).

front: Motors shut off but PF capacitors stay on. Result?
back: The plant goes leading; voltage can rise. Banks are often switched with the load or automatically.

front: Series vs parallel R-C: what changes?
back: Series: current shared, Z = √(R² + Xc²), PF = R/Z, bigger C → more resistive. Parallel: voltage shared, Z = R·Xc/√(R² + Xc²), PF = Z/R, bigger C → more capacitive.

front: 40 Ω ∥ 132.6 µF on 120 V, 60 Hz: first step?
back: Convert C to Xc: 1/(377 × 0.0001326) = 20 Ω. Then Iᵣ = 3 A, Ic = 6 A, Iₜ = √45 ≈ 6.71 A.
